title: Original Rags on the General records and the tune Mr. Joe
summary: Morton asked for Carew's copy of Original Rags and was held back on the record; Mr. Joe was Morton's tribute to Joe Oliver.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: Well, he, I think he, I think he had a greater scope, if you want to call it that, of any kind of, anything you wanted to pick up, you know, and play it. He, in that, on those general records, the, the, uh, Original Rags, I don't know how they happened to hit on that, but I got a letter from him, he asked me if I had a copy of Original Rags, the boy wanted him to record, to record his version of Original Rags. And I said yes, and I sent it up to him. So, afterwards, when I was listening to the records, he says, he says, if they'd let me go on that record, he says, I certainly would have tore it up, he says, but they held me down on me. Yeah.
Well, he played more like a Joplin, didn't he?
Well, he stuck, he stuck close enough, he stuck close enough to Joplin, yeah, that's, that's what they wanted, too, you know. Yeah.

Well, you know, that's a beautiful thing, though. Oh, it is. Original Rags, it's very nice. One of the nicest things, I like that Mr. Joe, where do you ever get the Mr. Joe tune, you know? Whose was that?
Well, it's Mr. Joe, it was, it was in honor of Joe Oliver, I think.
Oh, it is. But, uh, it's not.
I don't believe I've ever heard that orchestrated for a band, you know?
